common_name: Skeena Cherry (Self-Fertile Late-Season Dark Sweet Cherry)

planting.note: Plant bare-root or container trees in late winter to early spring while dormant, in deep well-drained soil and full sun.

directions: Skeena was released from a British Columbia breeding program and is prized for its large, firm, dark mahogany-red fruit with excellent flavor and good resistance to rain-cracking. It is self-fertile and ripens about a week after Bing, extending the mid-to-late season sweet cherry harvest for home orchards. Give it deep, well-drained soil, full sun, and consistent moisture as fruit sizes up to avoid splitting. Prune to an open center or central leader in late winter and net trees as fruit colors to deter birds.
sources: Summerland Research and Development Centre, Agriculture and Agri-Food Canada

common_name: Regina Cherry (Crack-Resistant Late-Season German Sweet Cherry)

planting.note: Plant bare-root or container trees while dormant in late winter to early spring; requires a compatible pollinizer cultivar planted nearby.

directions: Regina is a German-bred late-season sweet cherry valued commercially for its very firm, large, dark-red fruit and outstanding resistance to rain-cracking near harvest, a common problem in humid climates. It is self-unfruitful and needs a compatible pollinizer such as Sam or Hedelfingen blooming at the same time. Plant in full sun with deep, well-drained soil, water evenly through fruit development, and prune annually to maintain airflow and fruiting wood. Its long hang time and firm flesh make it a favorite for growers wanting to spread out the cherry harvest window.
sources: University of California Fruit and Nut Research and Information Center

planting.note: Plant bare-root or container trees while dormant in late winter to early spring; requires a compatible early-blooming pollinizer.

directions: Chelan was developed by a Washington State tree fruit breeding program and is grown commercially for its dark red, firm fruit that ripens roughly a week to ten days ahead of Bing, making it one of the earliest good-quality dark sweet cherries available. It is self-unfruitful and needs a pollinizer such as Black Tartarian or Index that blooms at the same time. Site it in full sun with deep, well-drained soil and protect the early blossoms from late frosts, since early bloom is both its advantage and its main risk. Water consistently as fruit sizes to reduce cracking, and thin overloaded branches to keep fruit size up.
sources: Washington State University Tree Fruit Research and Extension Center

common_name: Attika Cherry (Early-Season Firm Dark Sweet Cherry)

planting.note: Plant bare-root or container trees while dormant in late winter to early spring; requires a compatible pollinizer.

directions: Attika is a German-bred sweet cherry from the same breeding program that produced Regina, ripening in the early-to-midseason window at about the same time as Bing. Its large, near-black fruit is very firm with good crack tolerance, holding up well on the tree through occasional rain before harvest. It is self-unfruitful, so plant a compatible early-blooming pollinizer nearby for a reliable crop. Grow in full sun with deep, well-drained soil, water evenly during fruit development, and prune each winter to maintain an open, productive canopy.

planting.note: Plant bare-root or container trees while dormant in late winter to early spring; self-fertile, so a second tree is not required for fruiting.

directions: Sunburst was released from a British Columbia breeding program and is one of the older self-fertile sweet cherries still widely planted in home orchards. It bears large, glossy red-black fruit at midseason with good flavor, though it is somewhat more prone to cracking after rain than newer firm-fleshed introductions. Because it is self-fertile it can be grown as a single tree, but yields improve with a compatible pollinizer nearby. Plant in full sun with deep, well-drained soil, water steadily as fruit matures, and prune annually to an open habit for good light penetration and easy harvest.
sources: Summerland Research and Development Centre, Agriculture and Agri-Food Canada

common_name: May Duke Cherry (Historic Sweet-Tart Duke Cherry)

planting.note: Plant bare-root or container trees while dormant in late winter to early spring, in well-drained soil and full sun.

directions: May Duke is one of the oldest named Duke cherries, a naturally occurring group of hybrids between sweet and sour cherry grown in Europe since at least the 1600s and long favored in English gardens. The medium, dark-red fruit is tart when it first colors but sweetens considerably if left to hang until fully ripe, making it useful both fresh and for cooking. It is partially self-fertile and ripens earlier than most sweet cherries, giving it its name. Plant in full sun with well-drained soil, and prune to an open vase shape in late winter to keep the compact, upright growth productive.

common_name: Valentine Bush Cherry (Cold-Hardy Romance Series Dwarf Cherry)

planting.note: Plant bare-root or container shrubs in early spring once soil is workable, in full sun; benefits from a second Romance series cultivar nearby for best pollination.

directions: Valentine is one of the University of Saskatchewan's Romance series dwarf sour cherries, bred from crosses of Mongolian cherry and sour cherry to withstand prairie winters far colder than most tree cherries tolerate. The compact, multi-stemmed bush produces good yields of large, dark red, sweet-tart fruit good for fresh eating, juice, and baking. Plant in full sun with well-drained soil; it tolerates poor soils and drought once established but fruits best with consistent moisture during ripening. Prune out older, less productive stems every few years to renew the bush and keep it fruiting heavily.

common_name: Crimson Passion Cherry (Sweet Romance Series Dwarf Bush Cherry)

planting.note: Plant bare-root or container shrubs in early spring once soil is workable, in full sun; benefits from a second Romance series cultivar nearby for best pollination.

directions: Crimson Passion is a University of Saskatchewan Romance series bush cherry bred as a sweeter-eating counterpart to Carmine Jewel, with dark red-black fruit that leans closer to dessert-sweet than tart. The dense, rounded shrub is extremely cold hardy and stays small enough for foundation plantings or edible hedges. Grow in full sun with well-drained soil; established plants tolerate drought and poor soils but yield best with regular water while fruit is sizing. Renewal-prune a portion of the oldest canes out every few years to keep the bush vigorous and productive.
